scenes.headline: How a 4B model hands you a game asset
scenes.sub: It writes a page, and the page writes the GLB
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Pivot! This model writes a web page, and that page writes the 3D file your game engine imports.

scenes.text: The model never writes the 3D file itself. It writes Three.js code, and the page's own exporter turns that code into a GLB.
scenes.say: The model never writes the file. It writes Three.js code, and the exporter inside the page turns it into a GLB.

steps.say: A short prompt and a fixed system prompt go in.
The model plans first, for about ten thousand tokens on average.
Then it writes one HTML page that builds the asset out of boxes, cylinders and spheres.
A button runs Three.js's exporter on the asset's group, and the browser downloads a binary GLB.
That file is what you import into Godot.

scenes.label: shipped GLBs pass the Khronos validator with no errors
scenes.say: I ran every validation GLB through the Khronos validator. All four hundred and seventeen pass, with no errors and no warnings.

scenes.credit: my render of the dataset's GLBs
scenes.title: But glTF units are metres

steps.say: But glTF units are metres. Next to a person, the merchant is three point three metres tall.
And the treasure key is nearly eight metres. Each asset is sized to fill its own camera.

left.title: As shipped
left.say: Every part of the asset is its own node, so the median asset costs ninety draw calls.

right.title: Merged by material
right.say: Bake the transforms and join the parts that share a material, and a static prop costs eleven.

scenes.text: The file is valid glTF. Scale, origin and draw calls are still yours to fix on import.
scenes.say: The file is valid. Scale, origin and draw calls are still yours to fix when you import it.

recap: The model writes code, not files
scenes.say: Code, not files. Valid, but not to scale. Rescale, fix the origin, and merge.
